drills.q: Two flops in one clocked block, assigned with `<=`. What do you get?
options: A shift register: the second flop takes the value the first held before
One flop, because the optimiser merges them
Two flops holding the same value
Undefined, because the order of the assignments is not specified
drills.why: Non-blocking assignment evaluates every right side before writing any left side, so both read pre-edge values. That models real flops, which all sample at the edge and drive shortly after.

drills.q: The same block written with `=` instead synthesises to how many flip-flops?
options: Two, since the code describes two registers
One, because both would always hold the same value and the optimiser
Zero, because blocking assignment is combinational
It fails to synthesise
drills.why: Measured: two $_DFF_P_ with <= and one with =. Blocking assignment writes immediately, so the second statement reads the value just written rather than the value held before the edge.

drills.q: Why does the language leave the execution order of two blocks on the same edge undefined?
options: To give simulators freedom to optimise
Because real hardware has no such order: the flops are separate devices
Because defining it would break backward compatibility
It is defined, and simulators that disagree are non-conforming
drills.why: The undefinedness is descriptive rather than permissive. Non-blocking assignment does not pick an order; it makes the order irrelevant by splitting evaluation from assignment into two phases.

drills.q: What makes an inferred latch appear?
options: Using `always @(*)` instead of `always_comb`
A signal that some path through a combinational block leaves unassigned
Assigning the same signal in two places
Reading a signal before it is assigned
drills.why: A signal not assigned on some path keeps its previous value, and keeping a value requires storage. The synthesiser supplies storage in the form of a level-sensitive latch.

drills.q: An `always @(*)` block assigns a four-bit output, and a `case` leaves two of its four selector values unhandled. What does yosys report?
options: One latch for the whole vector
A latch for each output bit that needed one, named individually
A syntax error
Nothing, because `case` has an implicit default
drills.why: Measured: two $_DLATCH_N_ cells for that design. Latches are inferred per signal, not per block, and the warning names each one.

drills.q: Why is an inferred latch usually worse than a flip-flop?
options: It uses more transistors
It is transparent while its enable is high, so it has no single sampling
It cannot be reset
It only works at low clock frequencies
drills.why: The lack of a single sampling edge is the problem. It also makes the circuit sensitive to glitches on the enable, which a clocked flop would simply not see.

options: It generates faster logic
It derives the sensitivity list, which `always @(*)` does not
It states your intent, so a latch inferred inside it is an error rather
It allows non-blocking assignment in combinational logic
drills.why: Both derive the sensitivity list. The difference is that always_comb declares the block is meant to be combinational, which gives the tool something to check against.

drills.q: `if (rst) q <= 0;` inside `always @(posedge clk)` synthesises to which cell?
options: `$_DFF_P_` with extra logic on the data input
`$_SDFF_PP0_`, a flop with a synchronous reset input
`$_DFF_PP0_`, a flop with an asynchronous reset pin
`$_DLATCH_P_`
drills.why: A reset checked inside a block that wakes only on the clock is ordinary data, so it becomes a reset input on the same flop. Measured.

drills.q: Moving the reset into the sensitivity list, as `always @(posedge clk or posedge rst)`, changes what?
options: Nothing, the two are equivalent
The flop itself: it becomes `$_DFF_PP0_`, a physically different device
Only the simulation behaviour
It introduces a latch
drills.why: Measured, and it is the point of the exercise: two correct designs that synthesise to different devices. You cannot tell them apart by behaviour in a simulator; you can tell instantly by reading the cell.

drills.q: Why does an asynchronous reset still need its release synchronised?
options: Because it deasserts at an arbitrary moment, and different flops would
Because asynchronous resets are not supported by most FPGAs
Because the reset signal is slower than the clock
It does not; that is the point of making it asynchronous
drills.why: Asserting without a clock is exactly what you want at power-on. Deasserting without one is not, because the recovery and removal timing is not met uniformly across the design.

drills.q: `always @(a) y = a & b;` What is the disagreement?
options: The simulator and the synthesiser both build an AND gate
Simulation leaves `y` stale when only `b` changes; synthesis ignores the
Synthesis reports an error
A latch is inferred for `y`
drills.why: Measured: it synthesises to a single $_AND_. The hardware is right and the simulation is wrong, which produces the worst class of bug: it worked in simulation and failed on the board.

drills.q: Two continuous assignments drive the same wire. Why is that worse than a double assignment in software?
options: It is not; the second assignment simply wins
A wire is metal, so two outputs on it fight over the voltage and can
It causes a race that resolves randomly at each clock edge
It infers a latch to arbitrate between them
drills.why: The failure is physical rather than logical. This is the same rule your Part II checker enforced when it refused a control word that enabled two modules onto the bus at once.

drills.q: `equiv_simple` proves a design matches a reference. Over what?
options: The test vectors you supply
A random sample of the input space
Every possible input, without enumerating them
The inputs reachable from the reset state
drills.why: It is a satisfiability question, not a simulation. The solver looks for any assignment that makes the two disagree, and failing to find one is a proof that none exists.

drills.q: When the equivalence check fails, what has the tool found?
options: That the design does not synthesise
At least one input assignment where the two designs produce different
That the design is slower than the reference
That the two use different numbers of cells
drills.why: It reports unproven equivalence cells. Cell count is irrelevant to equivalence: two designs with wildly different cell counts can be proved identical in function.

drills.q: What single question is behind blocking-versus-non-blocking, the inferred latch, and the choice of reset?
options: Which optimisation level the synthesiser is using
Whether the design meets timing
Which of the two kinds of logic, combinational or sequential, this code
Whether the code is portable across vendors
drills.why: Each bug is that question answered accidentally rather than deliberately. Synthesising the design and reading the cells answers it precisely, every time, and costs nothing.
